title: Lifeng Ren
text:
I am a Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Applied Economics at the University of Minnesota, specializing in environmental and resource economics.
My research draws on large-scale household survey and Earth Observation data. Using applied econometrics, machine learning, and spatial analysis, I study (1) how households respond to environmental and climate-related hazards, including air pollution, drought, and wildfires, and (2) how public agencies can design more effective information systems and land use policies to help households mitigate the impacts of these hazards.

title: Lifeng Ren
text:
† “Public Provision of Air Quality Forecasts: Access, Accuracy, and Household Avoidance” (with Qingyin Cai, Qingxiao Li)



Under Review  [ Abstract | Working Paper ] 


Do air-quality forecasts help households avoid pollution exposure? We link nationwide household transactions to daily PM2.5 and archived EPA AirNow forecasts during 2004–2019, exploiting staggered forecast coverage and wind-driven pollution transport. Coverage, which bundles forecasts with current air-quality information, doubles the response of store visits to PM2.5. Households with access shift shopping ahead of high-pollution days and respond more when recent forecasts are accurate. Raising recent accuracy from its mean to the 75th percentile cuts exposure by 26 percent of the access effect. Gross shopping-channel mortality benefits are about $16 million annually, before accounting for exposure from rescheduled trips.





† “Agricultural Adaptation to Drought: Evidence from Vietnam” (with Giang Thai, Khoa Vu, Nguyen Vuong)



 [ Abstract | Working Paper ] 


We study how drought shapes agricultural adaptation through the reallocation of land and inputs in Vietnam. Using a long difference approach, we find that in the long run, drought reallocates land away from rice toward other crops, while the shift toward aquaculture depends on local water conditions. Our mechanism analysis shows that drought persistently reduces rice productivity. Irrigation infrastructure mitigates the contraction of rice and facilitates crop diversification, while electricity access enables mechanization in aquaculture. We also find that drought is associated with a shift of labor from manufacturing into agriculture, where it is absorbed primarily by crop cultivation rather than aquaculture. Our findings shed light on how infrastructure and local factor markets shape farmers’ long-run adaptation margins.





† “Distributional Equity of Land Use Change and Ecosystem Service Gains under Global Biodiversity Conservation Scenarios” (with Elliott Woodhouse, Justin Johnson, David Leclère)



Abstract


Global biodiversity conservation pathways require large scale reallocation of land from agriculture toward restoration, yet how the resulting costs and benefits are distributed across countries remains poorly understood. We downscale land use projections from four integrated assessment models to 10 arc second resolution, estimate spatially explicit changes in carbon stocks using InVEST, and evaluate distributional outcomes across five socioeconomic dimensions through the Applied Justice Taxonomy and Assessment (AJUST) framework. We find that natural land and carbon stocks are already unevenly distributed at baseline. Under the most ambitious scenario, carbon sequestration efficiency improves but restoration burdens remain concentrated in tropical regions where vulnerability is highest. Inequality in per capita ecosystem service gains remains high across all scenarios, with Gini coefficients above 0.84. Vulnerable groups, including low income and high Indigenous Peoples’ and Local Communities’ land share countries, face higher restoration costs and less favorable balances between burdens and gains. Utilitarian, egalitarian, and prioritarian perspectives yield distinct evaluations of the same outcomes, demonstrating that no single framework is sufficient to assess the fairness of conservation pathways.
